title: How does IKEA come up with names for its products?
author: NaOH
tldr: IKEA names its products with real Swedish words chosen by category, such as place names for sofas and men's names for bookshelves. Each name must pass a check for bad meanings in other languages. The company names 2,000 to 3,000 new products a year.

keyPoints: Founder Ingvar Kamprad had trouble remembering product numbers. He gave products names instead. A practical workaround became part of the brand.

Rule one is that products get Swedish names. They are real words, often inspired by places, nature, emotions or everyday expressions. Each category gets its own kind of word: Swedish places for sofas, men's names for bookshelves, animals and nature for children's products.

A candidate name must be a real word of 4 to 12 letters and pleasant to say. It should preferably contain Å, Ä or Ö. It must never be trademarked or a surname. IKEA says it checks every name for unwanted meanings in other languages and for political or religious associations.

Rule two is that services, functions and customer communication use plain descriptive names in the local language. The exception is a handful of Swedish words kept on purpose: hello, bye, welcome, welcome back and coffee.
IKEA names around 2,000 to 3,000 new products every year.
article.whyItMatters: The page is short and the summary covers nearly all of it. Open it for the exact wording of the naming rules, which commenters spent much of the thread testing against real products.

comments.overview: In a playful, sprawling thread, commenters from a dozen language backgrounds reported IKEA names that are rude or silly in their language. That made the article's claim of careful screening the running joke. The serious arguments were about whether Swedish names help or confuse shoppers, how to pronounce Swedish letters abroad, and whether IKEA quality has fallen.

themes.title: Names that got past the screening
themes.synthesis: Readers listed names that got past the screening, including the JERKER desk, GUTVIK bunk beds, VIREN toilet brushes, TRAMPA mats and FARTFULL workbenches. SVALKA wine glasses carry Baltic slang for a promiscuous woman, and HOVEN means excrement in Czech, which produced a 'Hoven sale'. Swedes replied that Ä makes SÄRNA a different word from Spanish 'sarna', and that SVALKA and JERKER may predate the rule, or even prompted it. Others pointed to deliberate puns, such as FEJKA for fake plants and LACK for a flimsy side table.

quotes.author: Markoff
quotes.text: So when IKEA had Hoven sale - Doprodej Hoven (Excrements sale), people were amused

quotes.author: tverbeure
quotes.text: I love the JERKER desk that I bought 26 years ago, so I assume this rule must be younger than that.

themes.title: Do odd names help or hurt shoppers?
themes.synthesis: Defenders said real names beat the ERP-code model numbers most firms use, and contrasted IKEA with confusing names at Sony, Microsoft and Shimano. Critics said foreign words are hard to remember, say or type, and near-identical cabinet doors with similar names are a warehouse nightmare. One reply blamed English spelling, since speakers of phonetic languages can pronounce and recall foreign names easily. Others noted GNOME dropped whimsical app names because users couldn't remember them.

quotes.author: designerarvid
quotes.text: Most companies name their products straight from the ERP system, creating incomprehensible codes that sounds like they come from Star Trek.

quotes.author: greatgib
quotes.text: good luck finding which white cabinet door you need to buy between VEDDINGE and VALLSTENA that are 99,9% the same, and have the same description on ikea website and shops...

themes.title: Å, Ä, Ö and pronunciation abroad
themes.synthesis: Asked why IKEA wants Å, Ä or Ö, most replies said it's foreign branding, the same trick as Häagen-Dazs and the metal umlaut. Swedes stressed that these are separate letters at the end of their alphabet, not accented A and O. A Swede in London complained that staff don't recognize product names said correctly, so he has to imitate an English mispronunciation. Others told him to treat it as funny and pointed out that English speakers will always read Swedish words with English spelling rules.

quotes.author: unwind
quotes.text: Å is a distinct letter, with a different and unique vowel sound. It is in no way "a slightly different kind of A".

quotes.author: thomashabets2
quotes.text: As a Swede in London, it's annoying that IKEA staff don't understand you when you pronounce the names correctly.

themes.title: The rules versus the catalog
themes.synthesis: Commenters checked the stated rules against real products. PAX has three letters, though it predates any formal rules, and MALM is a common Swedish surname. One Swede argued the real rule must be 'no names that are mainly surnames', since many Swedish surnames are ordinary nouns. Doubts about 2,000 to 3,000 new names a year faded when a reply cited a 35,000-product dataset and IKEA Canada's figure of 12,000-plus.

quotes.author: BambooleanLogic
quotes.text: A completely literal "No surnames, ever" rule would probably be quite a bit too restrictive. I suspect that the actual internal rule is "No names that are primarily (or solely) surnames", or something to that effect.

themes.title: Has IKEA quality dropped?
themes.synthesis: A side argument said IKEA has become fast fashion for furniture, citing replaced kitchen tools and new pieces that yellowed within years. Many replies disagreed from experience: decade-old LACK tables, furniture moved and rebuilt many times, and pricier brands that fell apart faster. A middle view held that IKEA sells across price points, from particleboard meant to last a few years to IVAR in solid wood.

quotes.author: whirlwin
quotes.text: You buy something one day, and it starts to deteriorate and become janky after a year, and you'll have a buy a new one. All products have gone through spreadsheet cost optimizations.

quotes.author: sdoering
quotes.text: It cost about four times as much as IKEA’s higher-end lines. After moving it from my mom’s place to my office, I can already see it falling apart after just three years

comments.consensus: The names are fun and good for the brand, and the article is a rare piece of clear corporate writing. Its promise of screening in every language doesn't hold up, since nearly every language group here found a rude name.
comments.dissent: A minority found the names a real nuisance: hard to remember, pronounce or tell apart when buying spare parts or matching cabinet doors. A Swede added that correct pronunciation doesn't work in IKEA stores abroad.

contrarian.author: bluebarbet
contrarian.text: The stuff lasts. Probably for a simple reason: Any given product line is bought by millions of customers, so design flaws are quickly found and remedied.
contrarian.why: Against the nostalgia for older, sturdier IKEA, this comment names a concrete reason current designs should be more reliable: huge sales volume.
